name: Yale Blue
lede: Yale Blue is the deep blue of Yale University, which a dictionary of colour calls reddish-blue, and it shares a place on the color charts with a crowd of older blue names.

sections.title: A university's blue
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary defines Yale blue as a reddish-blue used as the distinctive color of Yale University [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates the name to about 1850 [2]. Our library also lists a Ridgway 1912 plate under the name, but that one is a much lighter blue, so the old chart color and the university swatch differ [2].

The swatch is a very dark blue, about six units from [[navy]], and near [[marine]] [2]. Paterson's word reddish fits it, as the hue sits slightly toward violet [1][2].

sections.title: A crowd of older blues
sections.body: The ISCC-NBS block that holds this swatch gathers dozens of names, many old [2]. Zaffre Blue and Enamel Blue are dated to about 1554 by Maerz and Paul, Smaltino to about 1550, Eschel Blue to 1726 and Dutch Azure to 1751 [2]. Several are names of smalt and cobalt glass blues, so the swatch sits in a family with a long ancestry [2]. The Japanese name listed for the swatch, Konjō-iro, means Prussian blue color [2]. Compare [[prussian-blue]] and [[cobalt-blue]], two relatives of a dark blue like this [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this one covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 28, led by Filippino Lippi's 1497 Joachim and Anne, at about a third of the picture [3]. It is far more common in the 1400s, six paintings at five times the archive average, than in later centuries [3]. The earliest match is Taddeo Gaddi's Madonna enthroned, about 1355 [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test [3].
